utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to you, Mr. Albiston. I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, are you ready to continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. If we could have P509 brought up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, this is a document that you were shown on Tuesday and you were asked to provide your observations about this document and you stated: "Well, in this document, General Cermak is giving permission or agreeing that people can move freely." And that was at page 23.809. I would like to go through this one step at a time with you. And, first, on its face in this document, General Cermak is not agreeing or giving permission. He is, in fact, ordering the civilian police and the military police to allow the free movement of civilians. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the text of paragraph 1 is granting permission for unhindered entry, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I take it from the word "yes" that you agree with me that it is an order?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says "order" on it. We discussed -- or I offered a view on its qualities as an order earlier on, and there was some discussion also, I think, on Tuesday about who actually had authority in relation to the granting of passes and permissions and free movement and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, again, my question was about this document on its -- on its face, and I think --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: On its face it says "order." I accept that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, could we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 3.88 you state that this document cannot simply be ignored. And you conclude: "It should, in my opinion, be interpreted in the light of General Cermak's acknowledged role in relation to the international community and to UNCRO in particular and his desire to be seen to be assisting them." And I'm not sure I quite understand what you mean by this. And I'd like to ask you: Is the view here that you viewed General Cermak as issuing these orders pretending to have more authority that he has, in fact, and due to his desire to be assisting the internationals. Is that what you're getting at here?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think to say that he's pretending to have more authority than he has, may be to imply, if I were to accept that, would be to imply that I thought there was something improper about General Cermak's conduct in relation to this matter. My interpretation of it is that it is -- he is acting with goodwill, attempting to achieve objectives which will be to the benefit of the international community and to the benefit of the reputation of the Republic of Croatia. He has written an order, and you see my comments, that whilst I am taking a view in my report that General Cermak did not have the legal constitutional authority to issue orders to the civilian police, nevertheless, it is a document which I have to address and not omit. And if I am to stand by my judgement, then I have to offer some explanation as to where this document fits. Now, it says "order" on it, and I say in my report that the phraseology in the document is consistent with what you would expect in an order in a disciplined hierarchical organisation. And it says "order" at the top. And it has a rubric, an introductory paragraph, which gives the explanation, the rational, for the order. I think it's fair to say just by writing the word "order" on a piece of paper it doesn't, in fact, give the piece of paper the status of an order any more than if I wrote on a piece of paper "royal proclamation" it would be a royal proclamation. But it does require respondents to notify me immediately when the vehicles are found. Unfortunately, it is undermined a little bit by not actually having an addressee --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Albiston, I think are you moving a little bit away from my question which was --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Seeing this document in the light of General Cermak's international role, and I think you answered that at the beginning --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, right, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. This is an important document in the case, and I would ask that, Mr. Albiston, be allowed to finish the complete answer in respect of this. It is useful to the parties; and I submit it is useful to the Chamber. I can go back to it in re-examination, but he should be allowed to finish his answer in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: He testified at length on this document in examination-in-chief, Your Honour, I just wanted him to focus on my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson is entitled to guide the witness to focused answers on what she specifically asked. And if there is any matter still remaining, then, of course, in re-examination, Ms. Higgins, have you an opportunity to hear what the witness would, apart from the focus of this question, would be able to tell us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. To address, specifically, the element of the question concerning the international community and whether General Cermak was being dishonest, I'm not imputing dishonesty to General Cermak in relation to his choice of words on the order. I think he was trying to do his best to get a result on behalf of the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And would you agree - would you not? - that this order has very similar format as P509, the one we just looked at a few moments ago?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could, please, have D504 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is the order from General Cermak transferring MUP officers to another building. And this document also has a very similar format to D303 that we just looked at. Doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes it does. I don't know whether it's important, but it says at the bottom that it's addressed to individuals rather than copied to -- or, rather, addressed to addressees rather than copied to addressees. But I entirely accept the Prosecution's suggestion that this is similar in its format and layout.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In light of the similar format between this order and the D303 and -- P509 and D303 and the fact that those two orders have nothing to do with the international community, I'd like you to explain why it is you think that D303 should be viewed in a unique way in terms of General Cermak's international role.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, is this -- it's not D303 that's on the screen, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, D303 was the one we just looked at. If you'd like to see it again, we can go back to --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the question is: Why do I think this is an important document?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No. My question is why you view this as having to be interpreted in light of General Cermak's international role when he issued other orders in a very similar format that had nothing to do with his international role.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I -- I understand fully the implications of why it is you think that this document should be viewed in a unique way in view of General Cermak's international role. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I base that on paragraph 3.88 -- 3.88 of your report where you say: "It should, in my opinion, be interpreted in the light of General Cermak's acknowledged role in relation to the international community and UNCRO in particular."

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So I'm basing it on what you say in your report.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I'm not sure whether it's being suggested that this -- this is a -- why the word "unique" is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see whether I can get things on track again. Mr. Albiston, it seems that you are, in 3.88, saying that the order should be "interpreted in the light of General Cermak's acknowledged role in relation to the international community." And you then give -- refer to some details of that document: "It's important to note that the order did not specify which individuals or how many individuals should be allocated to the task. It made no attempt to give guidance on how any inquiry should be carried out and is, in my opinion, consistent with General Cermak's role as a coordinator." You say that is his role. And I see -- in the format of this order, I see weak spots, at least you see flaws, which, apparently, are a reason or are among the reasons why you interpret this document in a certain way. What Ms. Gustafson does at this moment, she presents to you an order in which she says, There's not much difference, as far as the format elements you refer to in relation to the other order, but the substance of it has got nothing to do with international relations, and, therefore, she is exploring how sound the format basis for your conclusions is. And that's why she puts the two documents in sequence to you. Ms. Gustafson, have I understood your intention?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I think mostly, Your Honour. I wasn't so much focused on what the perceived flaws were in the order were; it was more the statement that it should be viewed in light of the -- General Cermak's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you referred to the format, and you say this order in its format is much similar but the substance is quite different.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I was -- aimed at the -- exploring the answer that this was an effort by General Cermak to get a result on behalf of the international community and comparing that to orders with a very similar structure that have nothing to do with the international community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well it could not be the aim that -- to satisfy the international community. Mr. Albiston, is it clear now what Ms. Gustafson asks you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think I understand the point. And I accept the point that this order refers to a matter in which General Cermak is seeking to assist the international community. And Ms. Gustafson wants to draw my attention to other documents which might be considered by the Chamber to be orders, depending on their view, which don't relate to the international community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, if you have any follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I think I'll just move to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, on Tuesday, you provided some testimony about this document, and you stated that you thought the meaning was clear at page 23833, but you said that: "In my experience, in a hierarchical situation, it is very difficult to address an order to two different individuals without specifying how you expect that order to be complied with." Now, these -- this order is addressed to two different individuals in two different hierarchical structures. But, to me, it is clear that General Cermak expected this order to be complied with. He expected the military police commander and the civilian police commander to form a joint team to find this equipment, and he left it up to those commanders who are, after all, the experts in policing matters, to figure out how to implement that task. Now, is that not a reasonable interpretation of this order?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think in part it is reasonable. But it doesn't -- it doesn't contradict the proposition which I put on Tuesday, which is that this would be a difficult order for people in two separate hierarchical chains to comply with. I don't say "impossible," because common sense and goodwill can achieve an awful lot in the absence of proper constitutional, legal, hierarchical arrangements.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, that's something that's inherent in issuing an order to people in different hierarchical organisations, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my experience, in military and policing hierarchies, orders from one to another simply don't exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see whether I understand you. Mr. Albiston, you said this is a funny order because it's addressed to two different people and they are even in different -- Now, could you tell us, if I, for whatever reason, think that I'm authorised to bridge a gap or to create a link between two persons in two hierarchical situations, well, let's say, I want A to meet with B to do something. How would you phrase that order? Just to A, just to B, or would you address the order to A and B and say, Please meet, or you have to meet and do together something? I mean, I see, in general, the point that you shouldn't say to A and B -- give them similar instructions. But if the specific content of what you want to achieve is that you want A to meet with B and to do something together, wouldn't it be totally logical to address that to both A and B? If you do it only to A, then B wouldn't know about it; if you only do it to B, A would say I'm not addressed by it. It sounds so logical to me that for the specific purpose here that the general observation that you shouldn't issue orders to two different persons, because that creates confusion, that, here, it perfectly makes sense and is logical.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think, with respect, that that is the way that police and military organisations work. I entirely accept that common sense and goodwill can make things work without always having to refer back up the line of command to the very top for authority to do things, and it's not just a question of the organisations that I've worked in and with. It might be more relevant to these proceedings if I were to cite an example in relation to this place and this time. And what I have in mind - it may not be a direct parallel, but it may help the Court - is the agreement reached between the United Nations and the Republic of Croatia in relation to the way that UNCIVPOL would work with the Croatian civilian police. And there's a document which is, I think, cited in my report, and it's certainly known to the Chamber, which, at the highest level, sets out the mechanisms for that coordination. And it shows that the coordination will start at the bottom. And that in the event of a disagreement at the bottom level, there will be referral upwards and so on. So these sort of arrangement can work. I don't say that different agencies can't work together; all I say is that police, in particular, always look for authority in the law or the constitution for the actions which they take. Police are trained to enforce the law and to obey the law, and it is a part of their culture always to look for a specific authority for what they do. And, I think, that is what gives rise to occasions in witness testimony, for example, when we have heard about various witnesses saying that they didn't take orders from General Cermak, and yet, counsel for Prosecution is saying, Well, actually, they may not have taken orders, but we see things happening which suggests that what General Cermak was suggesting to them, that passing on information from the international community or discussing the situation, actually produced some sort of concrete results. I think those are entirely consistent positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to move, now, to paragraph 3.90 of your report, where you discuss General Cermak's 12th of August, 1995, request to General Gotovina to inform HV unit commanders in the Split Military District of the need to urgently return missing vehicles and equipment. And that's D304.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could have that brought up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you note in your report that the letter states that General Cermak has attempted to find and return these vehicles through the assistance of the civilian police and military police and has had no success to date. And you conclude that this is: "A persuasive indicator of the severe limitations on General Cermak's authority and influence over the police and army." And on Tuesday, you testified about this document as well at page 23835 and you stated: "It seems to me, from the text of the document, that it is tantamount to an admission by General Cermak that actually he is not getting anywhere with the steps which he has taken and that he realizes that if he wants action from the military, in relation to recovery of the vehicles, then it's to the Military Command that he needs to go." Now, in relation to the police, General Cermak is not asking General Gotovina to assist him in having the civilian police or the military police act in relation to this matter. It is clear, as you stated, that he is asking General Gotovina to take steps through his operational command. And this document certainly indicates that the missing equipment has not yet been recovered. But there's no indication in this document that either the civilian police or the military police have not acted on General Cermak's order, is there?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if General Cermak had considered that what was needed here was to have the military police and the civilian police take some further action that he thought they were not taking, then he would have requested assistance from somebody who he thought could initiate further action by the military police or the civilian police, wouldn't you think?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I -- I think I see the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In other words --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. The document does not suggest that -- if Prosecution is saying the document doesn't suggest that General Cermak has simply given up on the civilian police as a vehicle for finding the stolen vehicles, no. I entirely accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Doesn't this document simply indicate that General Cermak is attempting to employ another avenue in order to find this equipment that hasn't yet been recovered?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Perhaps this is outside of your expertise, and if it is, please indicate that. But the fact that General Gotovina acts immediately on General Cermak's request is an indication of a significance influence that General Cermak is able to excerpt at the level of the Military District Command. Don't you think? And, again, if you don't feel capable of answering that, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hesitate to comment on the relationship between the two Generals, who, as I understand, were of equal rank within the -- within the army. But I think -- I mean, if it helps, then, there is another document, which I cite in my report, which shows General Gotovina taking immediate action in response to General Cermak's request, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, you state in paragraph 3.90 that stolen vehicles should be a police matter. Now, I -- it's certainly outside the scope of this report, and I would think outside of the scope of your expertise to assess the extent to which the duties of military commanders might be triggered here in relation to equipment in the hands of their subordinates. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The remark in my report is simply intended to mean that, when Brigadier Forand reported this matter to General Cermak, he was complaining that his vehicles had been stolen. And that's a crime, and that's why -- well, one of the reasons, I think, why General Cermak involved the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, also in paragraph 3.90 you refer to Exhibit D500 and D502 which are documents that the Knin police chief Mr. Mihic wrote to neighbouring police station chiefs seeking the assistance to recover stolen vehicles and referring to a criminal complaint from the Knin garrison. And you were asked some questions about these documents on Tuesday, and I would just like to read some of those questions and answers to you. In relation to D500, you were asked: "What I'm interested in is its relevance in terms of the authority or not of the original orders which you saw from Mr. Cermak." And you answered, and this is page 23836 and following: "The way I read this document is that Mr. Mihic, the commander of the Knin police station, is ensuring that information he has received from General Cermak regarding the stolen vehicles is available to the other police stations so that, should these vehicles be found, they can be returned accordingly." And then you were asked: "Does it tell you anything about Milos Mihic's attitude towards the original order or not?" And you answered: "He uses the expression gathered information. He doesn't suggest that he is acting on the instructions of the garrison commander." And in relation to D502, you were asked again about its relevance to the issue of authority of Mr. Cermak, and also how Milos Mihic interprets the information as best you can say, if at all, that he received in respect of the order. And you answered: "In part, Mr. Mihic is regarding General Cermak as the vehicle for conveying information about a crime from the complainant and into the civilian policing system."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could please move into private session for my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 3.93 of your report, you refer to General Forand's letter to General Gotovina, the 26th of August, which is D150. And you state in bold highlighted text: "Brigadier Forand had come to the conclusion that General Cermak did not have the authority to deal effectively with this problem." And you refer to General Forand's statement in that letter: "I am sure that he is very frustrated to find that his authority is limited in certain areas." My question for you is: Are you aware of the specific facts and circumstances that formed the basis for General Forand's conclusion that he was sure General Cermak was frustrated to find his authority limited? Do you know the basis for that conclusion in his letter?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what -- what you're alluding to, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So I take it you didn't review General Forand's testimony in that regard?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read General Forand's testimony. I don't remember the particular issue, in relation to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So you didn't -- that's not something that you incorporated, certainly not explicitly, but even implicitly in your report and the conclusions that you draw?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't cite any testimony from General Forand. No, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I would just refer the Court to transcript pages 4235, to 36 here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, these written orders from General Cermak to the civilian police span a period beginning in early to mid August and extend into October. Now, that suggests - does it not? - that General Cermak held the belief and continued to hold the belief that he had the authority, in fact, to issue orders to the civilian police. Does it not?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that that argument can be sustained from all the evidence. Certainly, during the period to which you refer, General Cermak continued to carry out his duties. And the number of documents which are addressed or copied to the civilian police and could reasonably be argued as orders are -- is pretty small, in my view. I don't dispute the dates which you're suggesting for General Cermak's period in office, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, could we move to P34, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, this is a Human Rights Action Team report for the 29th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 2 in both the English and the B/C/S, under point five.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And it describes a meeting that the team had with General Cermak. And starting in the -- the first paragraph under point five.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Perhaps we could blow that up. It's not very large.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Starting in the middle of the paragraph the report states: "While denying that anyone is being urged to leave their homes, the HRAT stressed to the general the necessity of providing a stronger Croatian police presence in outlying areas. The general stated he is giving an order to that effect today to Knin chief of police Romanic." My question here is similar to one I asked you yesterday: Do you think this statement reflects a genuine believe on the part of General Cermak that was, in fact, able to issue orders to the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my concern is that we are going to documents and questions are being posed in respect of Mr. Albiston's view of what other individual believed at the time. And I think we have to be very careful about drawing conclusions about other individual's beliefs. There's only a certain extent that one can draw from this documentation. One can look at the actions that were taken, but it doesn't necessarily mean that an individual believed or didn't believe. And, therefore, I'd ask that caution be exercised in asking Mr. Albiston his view on Mr. Cermak's beliefs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the witness has been opining as to General Cermak's intentions with respect to certain statements he's made, so I think it's a fair question in that light.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, in view of the content of the report, the Chamber certainly allows you to ask the witness to draw conclusions but, at the same time, that some caution is well placed here is -- is true as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, if could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It certainly reflects a desire on the part of General Cermak to persuade the people whom he is addressing that he will take strong executive action. Whether that reflects his inner state of mind, I'm not sure that I do agree with that. It's right to tell the Chamber that my views may be influenced by having read what General Cermak said in interview with the officials of the OTP. But, nevertheless, as Document P34 stands, it seems to me to be an indication of what General Cermak wanted the people he was with to believe rather than what he believed himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Just to go back to something you said. I'd just like to confirm that you have, in the course of preparing your report, read General Cermak's interviews with the OTP and his statements in those interviews have influenced your views as they're expressed in your report. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they haven't influenced my views in relation to what did or did not happen. But there are a couple of paragraphs within the report which suggest what General Cermak wanted to tell the Office of the Prosecutor at the time of the interviews, and that -- I mention that to the Chamber in case they want to draw any conclusions about my view of General Cermak's position from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So you accepted the views that General Cermak expressed in his interviews with the Prosecution, as to what he wanted and desired at the time.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I'm not making a judgement about what General Cermak said. I'm indicating to the Chamber that I'm aware of what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And they influenced your views?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the sense that I took them into consideration along with all the other material which I studied, yes, I suppose they did influence my views.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Albiston, I'd like to ask you a question based on your personal experience as a police officer, police official. Now, if you were in a situation where you were working in coordination or cooperation with another person who you considered not to have the authority to issue orders to you, and that person tried to issue orders to you, would you take that up with your chain of command? Would you raise it with your superior officer, for example.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you haven't seen any evidence of anyone in the Knin Police Administration complaining or questioning General Cermak's authority to issue orders to them, have you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And are you aware that Mr. Cetina recently testified and stated that neither Mr. Romanic nor Mr. Mihic complained to them about General Cermak orders or sought his advice as to how to deal with them? I'm referring to pages 23526 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that Mr. Cetina gave evidence recently, but I haven't -- I didn't watch him giving evidence, and I haven't seen any indication of the evidence. And, of course, I accept what counsel says about what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, from my reading of your report, you have not considered this as a factor, this evidence of a lack of complaints or queries regarding General Cermak's ability or authority to issue orders. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's right that I haven't addressed the issue of what certain witnesses or concern officers said about this matter at the time. There are issues about chain of command which are addressed in relation to other matters, but not specifically to the Knin police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to move now to paragraph 3.50 of your report. And this is where you begin to discuss the issue of the -- General Cermak's role in the issuing of passes and freedom of movement. And in the second half of that paragraph, you rely on document D494.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could bring that up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you've concluded: "This document shows that the MUP considered that General Cermak had no authority over the movement of civilians." That's the last sentence of paragraph 3.50 of your report. And I'd like to ask you what, specifically, in this document, caused you to conclude that the MUP considered that General Cermak had no authority over the movement of civilians?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the authority for that, on this particular document, taking it in isolation, although I don't think it's best to read the document in isolation, but taking this document in isolation and the way that you have put it to me, then I rely on the last part of the handwritten section, which says: "It must come in writing" -- in translation it says: "It must come in writing from the MORH, Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia." In other words, General Cermak should annul what he said previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In relation to the movement of civilians, this document indicates that General Cermak has the authority to issue an order for the free movement of civilians - does it not? - in particular, the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've interpreted this in the light of other documents as meaning that he is cancelling that, because the Ministry of the Interior is saying, Well, We don't really accept that he has got this authority. And certainly in relation to civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, you -- the person who wrote this by hand -- and I assume you don't know who that is?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That person, at least on the face of this document, appears to consider that General Cermak has the authority to order the free movement of civilians, does it not?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not clear to me what form any order would take.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, we've seen, in fact, that that very day, General Cermak did issue an order for the free movement of civilians, than was P509 that we looked at a few moments ago. And there's no evidence - is there? - that anyone in the MUP thought that General Cermak didn't have the authority to issue P509 at the time, is there?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we did look at the evidence of a discussion on what the views of the MUP were about General Cermak's authority in this area, and I don't -- I don't want to repeat what I said then. What I can say is that I do not know what is the statutory authority for anybody to issue passes or to restrict movement. I can't tell this Chamber what that statutory basis is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, I was just asking you whether the -- to confirm that you haven't seen any evidence that anyone in the MUP thought that General Cermak didn't have the authority to issue P509 at the time. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I'm not sure that I can relate the subsequent material concerning the MUP's views of freedom of movement with the document which you suggest, yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to look at other documents now, so perhaps it would be a good time to have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is, Ms. Gustafson. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I explained yesterday, under what conditions the Chamber was considering to -- to adapt the scheduling next week. Has there been any commitment or any -- Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, Your Honours, good morning. Yes, we have -- I have discussed with all parties involved, and there definitely is a commitment. There is also an expectation that the testimony of the witness will be completed by Wednesday. And it seems that it could even start tomorrow, given current estimates. And if that is the case, then it is even likely that we will not need for the Chamber to consider sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis just with the approximate five sessions on Monday, the approximate five sessions on Tuesday, and the, perhaps, extra session on Wednesday will be sufficient to cover the examination of all parties. If I have misspoken or misrepresented anything, I'm sure my colleagues across the well will correct me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no corrections. I think the Chamber spoke about commitment, and you spoke about exceptions, which is not exactly the same, although with a firm commitment. Of course, we would expect then that it would -- and, of course, I'm aware that a commitment is always to some extent, conditional, that you never know what happens in a courtroom. But I understand the exceptions and also giving up the 15 bis time as a commitment by all parties, that, unless, totally unexpected things will happen, that the parties have divided the time in such a way that we can be confident that the testimony of Mr. Deverell will be finished by Wednesday, not later than 4.00. Then, Mr. Registrar, I think we still need a number to be assigned to the statement of Witness AG-10 for which protective measures were granted yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1782.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted -- no, was, I think -- yes, I think it was already admitted by written decision of the 16th of September, so -- but the statement now has got a number as well. The Chamber understands that, in relation to the issue of the admission of Milosevic and Martic material, that there's an ongoing discussion with the OTP. Are there any results to be reported already? Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Not any further than when we were last time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which was on the 28th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think the project is being considered by the OTP as to -- how best to manage it and provide the information. That's where we are, and Mr. Waespi is dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes, is he not here right now. But we have looked at it, and I think there has been some exchanges in dealing with the -- with the volume of information and how best to admit those without having all the witness statements. And I think there is an agreement that has been reached on principle, it's just a matter of sorting out the mechanics of the filing and how to resubmit the matter which, hopefully, we will be able to complete shortly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Can I assist the Chamber as well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: -- as to say that in terms of the motions that the Chamber received concerning the Martic and the Milosevic material, the text has now been agreed, in a table form, and it just needs to be effectively tidied up. But we have reached agreement on that part. We are still, as Mr. Kay says, awaiting further disclosure in relation to witness statements which we have not referred to from our own searches but will be coming, I hope and anticipate, from the Prosecution. So we are still in discussions with the Prosecution on that front.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on disclosure rather than on admission?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there are any obstacles to be expected, of course, the Chamber would like to be informed about it. Because we are reaching stages of these proceedings in which we cannot afford anymore to say that we are dealing with matters. Matters are at a point that they have to be resolved. So the Chamber is -- we'll hear from the parties both on a table of facts and on any possible problem in relation to disclosure of statements from these cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not in relation to those cases; it's the wired disclosure that is outstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The Martic/Milosevic has all been taken care of. It's the other, wider information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I -- yes, misspoke, Mr. Kay --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and I appreciate your correction. Then we can continue the cross-examination of Mr. Albiston. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hedaraly, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: While the witness is brought, Your Honour, I should just put on the record that I misspoke at page 32 of today's transcript. I had attempted to refer the Court and the parties to General Forand's testimony at pages 4325 to 26, and my colleague, Mr. Kehoe, helpfully pointed out that I had made a mistake. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm a bit surprised because I still have on my screen, because I'm used to checking all the references, I still have 4325 on my screen. So that apparently was the -- what you referred to at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My dyslexia persists. I meant to refer to 4235 to 36, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 4235, 4236, which makes any questions as to the page I have on my screen superfluous. Let me just check. Ms. Gustafson, are you ready to continue the cross-examination of Mr. Albiston?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. If we could have D499 brought up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, this is an order that you testified about on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could move to page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It's an order from Mr. Moric to the police administrations, dated the 17th of August. And, among other things, it states: "Do not restrict the movement of European Union monitors, UNCIVPOL members, or UNHCR members." And on Tuesday you stated at page 23818: "In my opinion, it demonstrates that the assistant minister for the interior, Mr. Moric, is the man who is making and communicating decisions about the requirements for passes, freedom of movement, and those sorts of issues within this area." And the contents of this order are similar to the contents of General Cermak's 15th of August order, except that this order relates to members of international organisations, and General Cermak's order relates to civilians. And right before the break, you confirmed that there was no evidence that the -- anyone in the MUP had thought, at the time, that General Cermak didn't have the authority to issue his order. And I'm wondering how you've concluded that it was Mr. Moric rather than General Cermak who was the man making decisions about freedom of movement, in light of these two distinct, rather similar, orders, albeit dealing with different subjects in terms of the people?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder, if were being asked to compare the two documents, if Mr. Albiston could be given a chance to just see just, again, the General Cermak 15th of August order, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Certainly, if that will help the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, I -- Ms. Higgins protects you carefully. If would you have any need to look at any document - and I think earlier you expressed your wish to see a certain document again - you are invited to directly address Ms. Gustafson or the Chamber so that we would never receive an answer by -- you would feel that you would have had insufficient opportunity to review a document again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, of course, Mr. President, I'm grateful for Ms. Higgins' protection. But, actually, in relation to the question, as I understood it, put by counsel, I would refer to yet another document. And it may that be that I can assist the Chamber without necessarily having the documents up on the screen, and the document to which I'm referring is one which was mentioned in the Chamber previously during the course of my evidence. I think during the course of my evidence in chief. And that was a document of, I think, the 3rd of August and it was from Mr. Moric and it described the roles of Mr. Tolj and Mr. Rebic in the arrangements for the issuing of passes. And earlier this morning, in answer to a question from Ms. Gustafson, I confirmed that I cannot refer to any constitutional order or legislation or authority of the type, which I have referred to in many parts of my report, which would establish exactly who has what authority to deal with this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I appreciate your evidence in this respect. I do not know exactly whether this was an answer to your question, Ms. Gustafson. If not, please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I take it - please correct me if I'm wrong, because I may have misunderstood your answer - that the reason you conclude that it's Mr. Moric rather than General Cermak is based on the formal legal structures in place at the time. Is that -- is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Except that, as I say, I can't refer this Chamber to a law which says it's the Ministry of the Interior and not the Ministry of Defence which deals with this issues. I don't know what the law is about passes in areas which have been the subject of a military campaign and the restoration of civil law and order.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then -- then maybe I would like to ask my question again, which is, how did you come to the conclusion that it was Mr. Moric rather than General Cermak who was the man responsible for freedom of movement in light of the fact that each of them had issued an order in this respect?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The basis on which I draw that conclusion is that the 3rd August document, if that is, indeed, the correct date, to which I referred, shows activity at Zagreb, which is at the highest level, and which includes reference to officials from the Ministry of Defence, so that that is the basis on which I say the documents from Mr. Moric carry greater authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now I'd like to go to document P957.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It's another document you looked at on Tuesday. And this was the ECMM report, referring to a complaint to General Cermak regarding a restriction of movement. And it's the paragraph 2 that's relevant here. And on Tuesday, at page 23817, you stated: "I think what that indicates to us is that at the time of this incident, General Cermak is recognizing the role of the -- what he describes or what the author of this document ... describes as the minister of internal affairs, in other words, the MUP hierarchy, as the authority which should have been dealing with this matter." And my first question to you is: Based on your experience and knowledge, in your jurisdiction, how many people do you know who are outside the formal Ministry of Interior structure who are able to call the minister of the interior directly to have an intervene in a policing complaint, and if you know who they are, if you could name them or identify them.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know any.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So, based on your experience from your jurisdiction, you would agree that this document illustrates significant influence and access on the part of General Cermak over the MUP leadership. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's exactly right. Influence and access, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And there's nothing in this document that indicates that General Cermak could not have intervened directly with the Knin police in respect of a restriction on movement, is there?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I -- I accept this document at face value.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has heard quite a lot of evidence of General -- of international monitors being stopped at police check-points and being able to call General Cermak who would intervene directly to stop the restriction. Did you see evidence of that in the material you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you don't refer to any of this material in your report. And I take it from that, that you didn't consider any of that to be relevant to General Cermak's factual authority over freedom of movement issues. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if -- if you say that there's no reference to any of that in my report, I have to accept that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And did you consider it irrelevant, then, to the issues you were addressing?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think I did consider it irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And how, then, did you decide -- what process caused you to decide not to address any of this material in your report, given that you thought it was relevant, or at least not irrelevant?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I accept that some of these incident may have a bearing on judgements about what you call informal authority that General Cermak may or may not have exercised. But I think, if there is no reference to this in my document, it was because I was trying to address the de jure position in relation to the matters we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I would now look to move to the part of report entitled: "The Investigation of Crimes and Other Irregular Acts." And that's beginning at paragraph 3.56. And, in this section, you have focused largely on a number of the applicable legal provisions, and you have concluded that the garrison had no role in the enforcement of law and order or the investigation and punishment of crimes. And that's at paragraph 3.69. And at paragraph 3.70, you conclude that: "According to law, the only duty General Cermak had in relation to crimes coming to his notice was to ensure they were reported through the appropriate channels." And you gave evidence to that effect, as well, on Tuesday at page 23819.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, first, in relation to General Cermak's duties, you have referred to his responsibilities as a senior representative of a state body and a citizen. And the laws that you refer to are the Law on Criminal Procedure and the Basic Criminal Law of Croatia. And that's at paragraph 3.71. And I take it from this that you have not considered it to be within the scope of your report or at least have you not addressed any powers, responsibilities, or duties that General Cermak may have had in relation to the military justice system and under the military hierarchy as a garrison commander and a senior HV officer. Is that --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I considered that that was a matter for a military expert to address.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And from your answers yesterday to my questions about General Cermak's appointment and tasks from President Tudjman, you have not considered any duties that may have arisen from the tasks and assignment he was given directly by the president. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: With not -- well, I saw no evidence that he was given any tasks in relation to this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in respect of the last question which my learned friend has asked, she states: "Have you not considered any duties that may have arisen from the tasks and assignments that he was given directly by the president. Is that right." I would ask - we've seen one document which my learned friend referred to as an example yesterday which was P1144 - if my learned friend has any other evidence to support her question, I would ask that it be shown to this witness, who has reviewed between 2 to 4.000 documents, that he be given the opportunity to see the evidence that my learned friend says exists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The witness made clear from his evidence yesterday that this was an area that he did not address at all in his report. And I don't think it is reasonable or practical for me to try and have him look at all of the relevant evidence and draw conclusions when this is an area he has never turned his mind to. I think my question was a fair one in that context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The Prosecution is alleging that an authority was given by the president to Mr. Cermak over the civilian police. Now, I ask that my learned friend follow through on her obligation to put her case and to allow this witness to see that or other documents, if they exist. It's a very simply point, and this witness should be given the opportunity, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I put that case yesterday. It's very clear that this is something the witness did not address in his report. It is not my obligation to educate this witness on all the material and have him draw conclusions afresh.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Well, I'd ask that -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins, you have objected. Ms. Gustafson has responded. You had an opportunity to reply. Ms. Gustafson now has given her view again. Let me see whether the Chamber can rule on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before the Chamber rules on the matter, Mr. Albiston, I would have a question for you. As far as the authority of Mr. Cermak is concerned, is it correct to say that you focused on the position of a garrison commander as you find it in legal instruments of different kinds and that you did not include, in your analysis of the situation, any authority assigned beyond those instruments, for example, by the president, whatever they may have been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's absolutely correct, Mr. President, because if my review of the documents I didn't see any additional authorities ascribed to General Cermak. I understand the Prosecution's line of questioning, but I'm unable to assist, because I'm not aware of any documents which would provide that additional authority to which Ms. Gustafson appears to be alluding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, yesterday, a document, P1144 - I think it was page 4, Ms. Higgins - was shown to you. That is a later conversation of President Tudjman with Mr. Cermak - I think it was 1999, if I'm not mistaken - in which they look back --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to what happened at the time. There a -- Mr. Cermak mentions with what mission he was sent or at least what tasks he was assigned by the president, and then the president adds one element to that. Ms. Gustafson -- Let me first ask you: You have no other knowledge about the assignment of the task, further to what was shown to you yesterday, or do you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't. And I remember the document which was shown to me yesterday, but I have seen nothing else which suggests the sort of authority which, clearly, Ms. Gustafson is suggesting to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, is it clear to you that the position of the Office of the Prosecution, is that due to this, let's say, personal assignment, if I could call it that, by the president, that the authority of Mr. Cermak went beyond what is written in legal instruments and that they interpret the behaviour and the acts and conduct of Mr. Cermak in that broader context? Is that clear to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It has become clear to me in the last two days. Yes, certainly, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And, Ms. Gustafson, in view of what the witness has told us he is familiar with and what he has no knowledge about, I think that you could phrase your questions in such a way that -- and the Chamber certainly does not encourage you to do that, without any specific need as to give this witness all of the evidence, that is, not only documents, documents that might not be that much, as a matter of fact, but other witnesses telling the chamber about the background of why Mr. Cermak was chosen for the job, what his specific qualities were. I think there's no need to put that to the witness at this moment. But, the Chamber will carefully listen to your questions, and the Chamber will also consider whether, due to the formulation of that question -- of your questions, that position will change. Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, arising from the comments that Your Honour has made, I don't want to prejudice the evidence that this witness is giving, but an important issue does arise, and I would ask, just for a couple of moments, that the witness be removed from the courtroom so that can I address you and Your Honours at the Bench in his absence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we would follow your wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour. I will are brief. The point that Your Honour refers to about the evidence that has been given before this Chamber from various witnesses as to how Mr. Cermak was appointed and what the remit of those roles, that I am not concerned with. What I am concerned is the specific allegation that has been put by my learned friend that a specific authority over the civilian police was given by the president to Mr. Cermak. Now my learned friend, Your Honour, has an obligation to put her case. She also has obligation to have a foundation, an evidential foundation, for the questions that she asks. And if it's not going to be raised with this witness, for the purposes of transparency, which I know Your Honour is inherently concerned about, I would ask that the Chamber ask Ms. Gustafson to provide me and my team with the documents that she refers to in relation to that specific point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first, perhaps, try to find out what Ms. Gustafson was exactly referring to. Were you referring to more than this -- what we find in this conversation between President Tudjman and Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm referring to the whole body of evidence, indicating factual authority by General Cermak over the civilian police --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, now we have to carefully make a distinction.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether that authority was or was not part of or included in what is described in a rather general way in this conversation, if you are referring to the exercise of -- well, just to say, You see here Mr. Cermak signs an order. That's something different from, Look, the president has assigned specific authority over the civilian police to Mr. Cermak. Now, finally, the Chamber, of course, will have to look at the evidence in its entirety, including what was said in this conversation, what happened on the ground, how persons receiving orders were interpreting them. There's a lot of evidence there. But I think that the primary concern of Ms. Higgins seems to that be, in the formulation of your question, it is suggested, more or less, that the assignment for specific tasks follows from documentary evidence, which the witness has not seen. Ms. Higgins, is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: That's absolutely right, Your Honour. It's that specific point, not the body of evidence, that my learned friend referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Gustafson, if you would -- I do not know to what extent for your line of questioning it is needed to refer to evidence or documents in which the president assigns an authority over the civilian police to Mr. Cermak, rather than, that, as we have seen in this conversation, the tasks assigned to Mr. Cermak, at least from the words spoken, seem to go beyond what is the -- the task of a garrison commander as laid down in legal, written instruments. Again, if you need a specific reference to documents in which an authority over the civilian police, in those words, is assigned, then have you to give it to the witness. If, however, you want to refer to the broader tasks assigned, often they're summarized internationals and restoration of order, in this conversation we find a bit more details in 1999. If you need to go any further, and, nevertheless, want to stick to assignment of authority over the police, then you'll have to show it to the witness. Is that clear? And perhaps we now go back to your question exactly. Could you ...

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- tell me exactly where --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure exactly where in the transcript, but the question was to have the witness confirm that he didn't consider, in the scope of his report, any duties arising from the tasks assigned to him personally by President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just see. Again, page and line, could you assist me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I ... Page 48, line 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's of some concern that we have to go back six pages to find where the question is. Yes. I think the matter is clear at this moment, isn't it, Ms. Higgins?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: It does clarify one point, although if I could raise the following issue: Yesterday, my learned friend asked the witness whether he had any reason do doubt that President Tudjman could have assigned General Cermak authorities, significant authorities, in any informal way rather than a statutory or legal procedural way, and she was clearly referring, although didn't put it directly, to the assignment to Mr. Cermak by the president in respect of authority de facto, de jure, whatever to Mr. Cermak from the president. And, again, I reiterate my request to the Bench that Ms. Gustafson, in the interests of transparency, indicates to this team what she is referring to beyond P1144.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that what -- Mr. Kay is looking at the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I can assist my learned friend because I've found the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The precise question was: "... from your answers yesterday to my questions about General Cermak's appointment and tasks from President Tudjman, you have not considered any duties that may have arisen from the tasks and assignment that he was given directly by the president. Is that right?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that means -- that's the same question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness apparently has considered the authority of Mr. Cermak in the context of the -- of the legal framework in which he was appointed and not anything outside that. Let's not now speculate. Because yesterday we see in P1144, nothing specifically is said about authority over the civilian police. That may be clear. So, therefore, if this was put to the witness yesterday, there was no specific reference to the civilian police. And under those circumstances -- but if you phrased the questions in such a way that a suggestion from that assignment, from the text used there, that that would include civilian police, apart from what happened on the ground later on, but also any suggestion whether it would be excluded, there's no way it's about tasks. It's about areas that President Tudjman and Mr. Cermak are talking about. Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour. Again, for the purposes of transparency - and I'm looking further down the line to the final brief stage - my concern was the words that were put "keeping order," "preventing disorder" and as Your Honour rightly says, there's nothing in here about authority over the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but it's also not excluded --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that the civilian police would play a role in -- I mean, the text doesn't say anything. But apparently Mr. Cermak, with -- who is appointed as a garrison commander, has, at least that's what they say at that time that in -- in 1995 that he was tasked, that's at least how I understand this line, tasked with a role in preventing or -- how do you say the ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: The words are "keeping order," "preventing disorder," which are, of course, open to interpretation and, finally, conclusion by the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: But I raise the point because it is one that I know, further down the line, will be an issue between the parties. And I want it to be put to the witness fairly if there's any other document that is relied on than this. Surely I'm entitled --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... he did -- he did not -- I do understand that he did not even consider -- he did not consider P1144, and he did, as I asked him, he did not consider the authority of Mr. Cermak beyond the scope of what a garrison commander, under the existing legal instruments, is tasked with.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, Your Honour. My point is a separate and distinct one, which is whether I can be given the documents that my learned friend is referring to when she puts her position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- that was the second --

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: That's what I would like, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the first thing you asked is that Ms. Gustafson would put to the witness certain documents. Now the second thing is that, Ms. Gustafson, if there is any document which is not yet in evidence because that's -- or not yet disclosed on which you rely for the authority granted, not under the legal instruments but by the president, to Mr. Tudjman [sic], anything which is not in evidence or not disclosed or where it could be unclear for Ms. Higgins that this was disclosed material which she would not have expected to deal with this matter, then could you tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, there's nothing that is not already in evidence. And if it assists Ms. Higgins, I'm relying on the large body of evidence that General Cermak's role was -- part of that role was the normalisation of life within the garrison which, in the Prosecution's submission, is not limited to turning on the lights and the water. And I would also refer, for example, to the interview he gave at P2355. If that assists my colleague, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Higgins, apparently there is not anything which you are not already not supposed to know in this context.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I'm grateful. And final, without wishing to repeat myself, even if it is in evidence, it is certainly unclear to me, and I give the commitment to knowing as best as anybody can know the documents in this case, what exhibited material my learned friend is relying on for the single proposition that President Tudjman assigned tasks to Mr. Cermak an authority over the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was not part of the question. Because the question did not specifically, if I -- I will check it again -- specifically refer to authority over the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour authority over the civilian police, that's fine. I would still like to know what exhibited material my learned friend is relying upon, because it's certainly unclear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that she's relying, written material, primarily on P1144, and, of course, there's other evidence which explains why and for what purposes Mr. Cermak was chosen by the president. And I do understand that the Prosecution wants to interpret what these tasks assigned to Mr. Cermak really meant by looking at what then happened on the ground, on paper, or in meetings, or under whatever circumstances, in interviews, in -- et cetera. That's how I understand the position of the Prosecution in this respect. If I'm wrong, please, correct me, Ms. Gustafson. But there's not a document somewhere where it says, Mr. Cermak, don't forget to keep tight control over the civilian police or don't let them off the hook if they're not performing well or -- There's nothing of the kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Not that I am aware.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that the matter has been sufficiently further explored. And Madam Usher is invited to escort the witness into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the flow of evidence could be interrupted as little as possible, that would be highly appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. And I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, we'll continue. Ms. Gustafson, perhaps you should repeat the question which was put to the witness or -- in the same wording or in a slightly different wording, because I wouldn't expect him to have a recollection of so many pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. And perhaps I could preface it by referring the witness to his answers yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: When I was asking you about whether you were in a position to say whether President Tudjman couldn't have granted General Cermak authority, in fact, in an informal way, of General Cermak over the civilian police, and you stated that you didn't know about the relationship between -- the informal relationship between the president and General Cermak and that you weren't, on the informal side, you said: "I'm not qualified to say" -- When I asked you whether you could opine on President Tudjman's informal authority over the structures of government, you said: "I'm not qualified to say." And I would just like to follow up on that. You have not considered it within the scope of your report or expertise to consider whether or not any duties may have arisen on the part of General Cermak arising from any informal tasks -- or tasks he was assigned in an informal way by President Tudjman. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is entirely fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And is it right that, in this section of your report on the investigation of crime, that you have only considered General Cermak's formal legal role within the MUP structure in relation to investigating crime, and have not addressed whether or not General Cermak could, in fact, initiate an investigation into a criminal incident?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't put it that way. I looked at the de jure situation and also at the de facto situation, where I conclude that he didn't have the resources at his disposal to deal with these matters. But I think it's quite clear from the law that garrison commanders don't play a role within the criminal justice system.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And when you refer to "resources at his disposal," you consider that he didn't have a sufficient personnel within the garrison unit to conduct an investigation. Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The garrison command itself, yes, doesn't have the resources to do that and isn't designed for it. Although, of course, it is probably better to hear an expert opinion on that from a military man. But so far as the relationship between the civilian police and the criminal justice system is concerned, I think can I say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to move, now, Mr. Albiston, to paragraph 3.71 of your report. And, in particular, the last sentence where you refer to documents indicating that General Cermak was passing and receiving information as part of his liaison role. And we looked at a couple of those documents yesterday, and I won't repeat that. I'd like to look at another of those documents that you cite here, which is D505.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could bring that up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, if I could also just direct your attention to paragraph 3.95 of your report where you refer again to this document. And you conclude that this document is an unambiguous declaration by General Cermak that, in the absence of any requirement to assist internationals in a liaison capacity, he did not deal with crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And is it possible to just bring up the English initially of this document. Is it possible to just show the English, initially. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you've stated that this -- the language in this document is not the language of a senior member of a hierarchical chain of command, issuing orders to subordinates.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
