utterances.text: And the tone of this letter is very different from the tone of General Cermak's written orders to the police. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you know if General Cermak signed this letter?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You don't know one way or the other?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I see commander of the Knin garrison at the bottom. But I haven't seen -- I don't have the original document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. We can look at the B/C/S as well. So you weren't provided with the original documents, just the translations. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no Croatian, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the B/C/S, if I suggested to you that that's not General Cermak's signature, you don't have any reason to disbelieve that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, not. I'm not familiar with what General Cermak's signature looks like, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you would agree that, in light of the fact that General Cermak didn't sign this letter, there's no indication that he necessarily chose those particular words or necessarily even saw the letter. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is it new information for me. And certainly it would be true that if General Cermak didn't sign the letter, then I'm not in a position to say what General Cermak's attitude to the language of the letter would be.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to a split screen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you can see that it relates to the theft of material from a factory in village called Srb. Do you know where Srb is?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't place it on the map, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So don't know whether it's inside or outside of the Knin garrison area?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And it is, in fact, in the municipality of Donji Lapac, which is outside the Knin garrison area. And did you notice that it was -- oh, I guess you didn't receive this document in the original, just the English translation. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just the English translation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, in fact, it's a two-page document in the original. And the letter that's being -- there's another letter attached to the English and I would just like do bring that up.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Which can 2D04-0153 ET. That's the doc ID number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is the letter that was originally sent to General Cermak, describing the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel. I believe we addressed this during one of our sessions, but this is the document that is misstated that hasn't been uploaded yet. We see that the original letter was September 19th, whereas the translation is August 19th. I may be mistaken, but I do recall we discussed this, Mr. President, or you brought it up, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I paid attention to a difference, and that difference in the date, and that I asked the whole of the document to be reviewed for translation, where, apparently such a mistake was made here.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I -- my understanding was that it was a Cermak Defence document and that they would be look into the translation, but perhaps I'm mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think, as a matter of fact, it was. But I'm not concern about that anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes, it was, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and have you reviewed the translation in other respects apart from the month?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can do it within the next minute or so if it helps the Chamber. I'm afraid my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, at this moment I asked to you do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed in the following way: At this moment, we understand that the English version gives a date which does not correspond with the other -- with the original. We'll proceed on the basis that -- we'll proceed on the basis that there are no other mistakes. But -- otherwise, we would have to wait and stop, which is not what I'd like to do at this moment. Let's proceed on the basis that the translation in every other respect is accurate, but if there will be any doubts, we will then here, within this one minute, from you, Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: I appreciate that. I understand it's the 15th of September that's the correct date. And we will check the rest of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, are you able to read this document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, I have on my screen now an English translation of a document which starts off: "According to the information at the disposal of our association ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. If you could read through that. And this is a document that has been sent to General Cermak from Zagreb, and it describes the alleged incident of equipment that was supposed to be taken from the factory in Srb to Zagreb but was, instead, fraudulently removed to a private company in Pozega.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And Pozega is in -- it's not in Sector South; it's not in the Zadar-Knin Police Administration; not in the Knin garrison area; it's in North-East Croatia. And my question for you is that -- the fact that this complaint is coming from Zagreb, that the alleged theft occurred outside the garrison area, and that the property is alleged to now be in a municipality in North-East Croatia, nowhere near General Cermak's area of authority, those would be relevant factors to consider in -- before drawing any inferences, in a general way, about whether General Cermak dealt with crime or had any command, in fact, over the civilian police within his area of responsibility. Wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly in relation to this crime, I entirely accept that proposition, although the previous document says - and I will try to quote from memory because it's not up. It says, We have no authority in this and similar matters. Which I read, in my reading of the document's English translation, to suggest that General Cermak was saying, Look, I don't deal with crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, a very practical matter: This document apparently is uploaded in e-court in, as it says, original language, English. I do not see any translation uploaded in e-court. Is there any ...

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, in fact, I was about to request that it be added to D505, which in -- D505 contains this letter in the original, and it was not translated in D505. So I would just like to add this to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then also have the date, perhaps, be verified, because it seems very much a 5 to me rather than a 3 in --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Certainly. And, Your Honour, if I could request that that document be added to the exhibit, and we will verify the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which means that we complete the translation of D505 so that it covers the whole of the document, rather than only one page of it. Mr. Registrar, is that clear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the translation of the second page of D505 is uploaded, then it will become the second page of the translation. And then we have - and that's new for us - then we have two pages with both problems with the date, in translation or in transcription. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, I would like to turn, now, to the part of your report entitled: "The Garrison Commander and the Prevention of Crime." And that begins at paragraph 3.72. And in that paragraph you conclude, in relation to General Cermak's subordinates: "... that his actual subordinates never exceeded ten in number; and there is no suggestion that any of [those] individuals were involved in any crime [sic]." Now, in -- you're referring here to his formal subordinates within the garrison; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm referring to the small number, the handful of people, directly subordinated to General Cermak according to the documents that have I read. Although I understand that the Prosecution's view of who might be subordinated to General Cermak is rather different.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the -- you've not addressed and, again, I would think that it would be outside the scope of your expertise to consider the extent to which units within the garrison might be considered General Cermak's subordinates pursuant to the provision of the service regulations that all units and institutions within the garrison are subordinate to the garrison commander as regards the issue of order, discipline, and service. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I touch on that tangentially in my introduction, but I leave firm conclusions and a more detailed examination to a military expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to go to the next paragraph of your report where you say, at 3.73: "An examination of the documents in the case reveals that responsibility for the prevention of crime lay with the Ministry of the Interior." And then at paragraph 3.76, you make a similar conclusion. You say: "Several documents demonstrate the serious approach which was taken to the problems of torching and looting." And you say: "This was considered to be primarily a matter for the Ministry of the Interior." Now, you do not appear to address in your report, and -- the existence or function of the military justice system, and I presume that's something that you considered also to be outside of your expertise. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, ma'am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the conclusion that the responsibility for the prevention of crime lay within the Ministry of Interior, I'd like to look at a couple of documents that you refer to in your report, and the first is D46.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If that could be brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And just so you're aware, I'm going to look at a number of document with you, and I'll just have you familiarize yourself with them and then ask you a couple of questions. And you can see here, this is -- Mr. Moric's 10th August letter to Mr. Lausic where he informs Mr. Lausic of cases being noted of "individual Croatian army members on liberated territory, stealing movable property, burning houses, and killing the cattle ..." And in the last paragraph: "While understanding the size and nature of the tasks that you have to contend with, we kindly ask you to take measures to eliminate these things." And the next document is D48. And this is Mr. Moric's 17 August letter to Mr. Lausic. And, again, he notes the problem of burning and looting, and he says: "The perpetrators," in the second paragraph, "the perpetrators of these acts, in most cases, are persons wearing Croatian army uniforms. Our information points to these persons who are formally and in effect members of the HV but that there are also persons who are not members of the HV." Then in the next paragraph he says: "The fact that the perpetrators wear HV uniforms completely blocks the work of the civilian police." And the next document is D49. And this is Mr. Moric's order to the police administrations. Again, noting the problem of looting and burning. And in the second paragraph stating that: "Most of these acts are perpetrated by individuals in Croatian army uniforms and the facts indicate that these individuals are formally and actually members of the army, but there are also individuals wrongfully wearing Croatian army uniforms." And on the next page he lists a number of measures including having the police administration chiefs meet with military police, battalions, requesting mixed barrier check-points with civilian and military police. And in point 5 stating that if military police cannot perform the task mentioned in item 4, which is to process the crimes, the civilian police will do it alone, irrespective of whether the perpetrator wears a Croatian army uniform? Now, I would like to briefly review the evidence of a few of the witness in this case, including Mr. Lausic, who testified that, in practice, after Operation Storm, the MUP would contact the military police at the first sign of a uniform. That's P2159, paragraphs 48 to 49, 55 to 59, and 62. And Mr. Buhin, whose testimony I understand you have reviewed, who stated that if someone in uniform was suspected of killing or looting, they could be arrested by the civilian police but then would have to be handed over to the military police. That's at 9922 to 23. And then stated that in practice detaining military personnel was impossible. He explained that the situation was very tense and dangerous, at page 9942, and that the civilian police were frightened that the military police would shoot at them if they interfered. That's P963 and page 9942. And he agreed with the statement of Mr. Moric in D48 that the fact that the perpetrators wear HV uniforms completely blocks the work of the civilian police. Now, my question for you is how you concluded that the problem of looting and burning lay -- the primary responsibility lay with the civilian police, when the information you cite and the evidence that you reviewed indicates that most of the incidents are being perpetrated by HV members in HV uniforms and that the MUP had a limited ability to effectively act to stop these -- or process these perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the primary responsibility for dealing with civilian -- civil -- civilian law and order issues rests with the MUP. I don't think it's in dispute that in many of the crimes which were being reported, the persons who were suspected of involvement were either HV members or persons wearing HV uniforms, particularly in the early stages of the period that we're looking at. And that, therefore, it was necessary to invoke the assistance of the VP in order to address these issues. I accept that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So when you say "an examination of the documents in the case reveals that responsibility for the prevention of crime lay with the MUP," would it be better to clarify that to be civilian crime?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, the investigation of crime, until such time as it's demonstrated, that in fact it doesn't involve elements over which the civilian police can exercise that authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Such as the fact that the persons is wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, such as the fact that the -- there is a suspicion that the person might be involved -- might be a military man, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm going move to another topic now, so if this is a convenient time for the Chamber for a break ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will have a break, and we will resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Albiston, I'd like to go back to paragraph 3.76 of your report, near the middle of the page, where you state: "When it became apparent that there were serious problems in the area, Assistant Minister Josko Moric turned on 17 August 1995 to the chief of the military police administration, General Mate Lausic." And we've just looked at the series of correspondence between -- from Mr. Moric to Mr. Lausic, D46 on the 10th of August, D48 on the 17th of August. And my question is: What specifically did you consider to be the serious approach taken to the problem of torching and looting by Mr. Moric between the 10th of August and the 17th of August, the two dates on which he complained to General Lausic about the looting and burning?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure that I follow the -- the question. Mr. Moric had, as I suggested previously, anticipated that there might be problems and had set in motion arrangements to deal with them, going back to, I think, the 3rd, possibly the 4th, but I think the 3rd of August. And the correspondence which I cite here is part of a continuing liaison between Mr. Moric and Major-General Lausic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm asking because you said "when it became apparent that there were serious problems in the area." And D46, Mr. Moric's 10th of August letter to Mr. Lausic, indicates serious problems in the area. And then there is a letter on the 17th of August, again, to Mr. Lausic, complaining. Again, are you aware of any step Mr. Moric took in between those dates to deal with the serious problem of looting and burning?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moric had made -- given the directions in the -- in the matter that I -- in the document to which I referred to, to civilian police to cooperate with the military police to deal with issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Those are the documents from before the operation. Is that -- is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is an document from before the operation, the 3rd of August, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And there is no evidence that you've seen of Mr. Moric instructing his subordinates to take steps to deal with the serious looting and burning that had become apparent in the area after the operation, until the 18th of August, in D49. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd need to look back at the documents again. But I thought we had discussed earlier documents. Wasn't there a mention of a 10th of August document?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, that was a complaint to Mr. Lausic. But in terms of taking steps, instructing his subordinates to take steps, your not aware of any steps he took in that regard until the 18th. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the 10th of August document indicates that Mr. Moric was familiar, to some extent, with what was going on, presumably on the basis of information that was coming through his chain of command which generated the action which he took on the 10th August in relation to seeking the assistance of Major-General Lausic. Because, if I recall accurately the document which we were looking at earlier, that discusses some of the problems in the area and indicates that some of the problems are connected with people in uniform and attempts to address it through seeking the VP assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to go to paragraph 3.82 of your report where you state: "General Cermak had no legal duty or role in relation to the prevention of crime, a matter which clearly fell to the MUP." And my first question, again: You have not considered or addressed, here, the role of the military police or military justice system in the prevention of crime. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have left that to the military experts. My view on it, insofar as it relates to civilian policing it that it was secondary, that the primary responsibility for crime matters lay with the civilian police. Clearly, as I think is understood here, where suspects were in the military organisations or, indeed, wearing military uniforms and purporting to be members of the HV, then, of course, yes, there was a role for the military machinery, the VP, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in terms of General Cermak's duties, it's not expressed here, but I -- I understand, once again, you're referring to those duties that you consider to have arisen from his position as a citizen and senior representative of a state body, as you've stated in paragraph 3.71. Is that --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And now I'd like to go to the section of your report, titled: "The Garrison Commander and the Punishment of Criminal Behaviour." And that begins at paragraph 3.83. And we've already gone into Cermak's role and ability in relation to the investigation of crimes, so I'm not going ask you any more questions about that here. I would just like to ask you a couple of questions about your conclusions on the Code of Military Discipline that you draw in paragraph 3.84. And you seem to implicitly conclude here that General Cermak could not impose disciplinary measures under the Code of Military Discipline for incidents that amount to a crime. And if I'm correct in my understanding, if you could explain the basis for that in the evidence and your expertise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, what I'm doing in this paragraph is acceding to the military expert the responsibility for dealing with the code of military discipline and alluding to it in passing because I think there may be parallels with the civilian police, disciplinary mechanisms, and, really, the point that I'm trying to get across is that the matters which I was considering were the grave crimes which were taking place in this area at the time and not really matters which could be dealt with as minor disciplinary matters. We're not talking about minor instances of drunkenness or falling asleep on duty by either policemen or soldiers. We're talking about completely different matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: But, again, do you or don't you seek to opine as to whether or not General Cermak could impose disciplinary measures for crimes?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in relation to the civilian police he couldn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm not asking about the civilian police. I'm asking generally.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that question is better for the military expert. I see that he had powers of discipline, and I put that in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I would just like to be clear that -- on this, you do not seek to opine as to whether or not General Cermak could impose disciplinary measures for crimes under the Military Discipline Code. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I said in my report is that he had powers of discipline, and I take it no further than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in various places in your report you have discussed the performance of the Croatian criminal justice system after Operation Storm in the areas affected by that operation. And I would just like to ask you a few questions about that. And in terms of your -- what you, in fact, looked at, I'd just like to ask you one question about that. In paragraph 1.5 of your report, you refer to your -- the purpose of your report, and you state that you were: "Invited to comment upon Croatian Ministry of Interior structures and any difficulties which might have faced the police at this time." Were you asked to about -- to address any specific difficulties, or were you just asked to look at the documents and see if you saw any difficulties?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The invitation was non-specific. It was based, as I recall, on my experience of policing in circumstances which are outside the normal civilian policing conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, when you did that, were you operating under the assumption that the police and the Ministry of Interior were genuinely attempting to address the problems of looting and burning and killing after Operation Storm, and then, just look at the obstacles that may have been present in -- genuinely undertaking that task, or did you address whether or not the police and the military -- Ministry of the Interior were, in fact, genuinely attempting to address the crimes in the area?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first invitation to me was, as I indicated a moment ago, very general, to consider the situation. In -- as a sort of post-conflict reconstruction period, what are the policing issues. Then, when I was provided with the documents, one of the documents or some of the documents I was provided with set out the nature of the indictment and the Prosecution pre-trial brief from which it became clear that the Prosecution took a certain view about the performance of the criminal justice system. So I was looking at documents which might either give substance to that view or contradict that view. Later on, I tried to focus more on how the documents, which might support or contradict that view, actually related to General Cermak and his dealings with the civilian police, because, obviously, the range of the documents is quite significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, just -- I take it from your answer - and correct me if I'm wrong - that you did address or you did consider the issue as to whether or not the Croatian authorities were genuinely attempting to address crime and that if you had seen evidence that they weren't, that would be something that you would have covered in your report. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's fair, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now in paragraph 3.59, you refer to the crime police. And you state that: "The minutes of the crime police departmental chiefs on 6 and 7 August 1995 show the procedures to be undertaken, when dealing with the dead bodies, including finger-printing and the arrangements for the admission of international observers to collection centres." Now, on the issue of the procedure to be undertaken with dead bodies, you are aware - are you not? - based on the evidence that you have reviewed, that a procedure was implemented after Operation Storm whereby dead bodies were treated as if they were combat victims, no on-site investigations were carried out in most cases, and the corpses were collected; identified, where possible; and buried without conducting an investigation to determine the cause of death. Is that right? Did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems clear to me from the documents that that happened on a significant number of occasions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, wouldn't that be something that would be significant, in terms of the performance of the Croatian authorities in investigating and punishing crime, the fact that large numbers of dead bodies were simply picked up off the ground and buried without an investigation?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that there are various reasons why that might have taken place to do with health, the heat, and so on. But as a professional policeman, I would certainly say that it would be highly desirable, in the event of finding bodies where there is a suspicion that the persons died through violence, to be able to conduct an investigation at the scene and a subsequent post mortem examination in controlled circumstances. The presumption in most police establishments is that where somebody has died through an unexplained cause, the case should be treated as a suspicious death and should be handled accordingly until such time as it can be shown to be something else. That is the ideal. In these circumstances, I think the ideal was not achieved as regularly as, from a policeman's point of view, it ought to have been. But that is the fact of the matter. There are examples, of course, which we can see where bodies were found and the procedures of which I, as a policeman sitting in an armchair hundreds of miles away, would approve; and there are other examples which seem not to meet the desired standards.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in light of your answer, why didn't you mention the fact that killing victims were not being investigated when you assessed the performance of the Croatian authorities in investigating and punishing crime after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because when I came to draft my report, I had focused my review and the areas about which I thought it appropriate for me to write on the direct locus, which I believed, from the documents, General Cermak to have had, in relation to these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, you've also mentioned in several places of your report resource constraints on the Croatian authorities. For example, in paragraph 3.115, you refer to an entry in the Knin police log that the police could not attend a reported fire in a house for want of a vehicle. And you've got a whole section on civilian police establishment and strength and another section on other police resource issues. Now, again, can you explain why you focused on issues such as deficiency of equipment and deficiency of manpower in assessing the performance of the Croatian authorities and didn't mention the fact that they weren't investigating killings?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as can you see from those sections which deal with these sorts of general issues, the sections are very short. I tried to set context for the other areas of the report which I thought were specific to General Cermak's role. And whilst I haven't gone into significant detail about the performance of the police, because I think, if I had gone down that road, there would have been several volumes to this report. I think I have tried to provide background information which is of assistance to the Chamber which shows that, in summary, there was a system that was gradually being established. I think I have been fair in describing some of the ways in which that system achieved successes in some of the investigations and prosecutions that were undertaken. And I think I have also drawn the attention of the Chamber to what I considered, from my professional perspective, to be some of the defects in that system.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And would you agree, now, that not investigating killing victims is a defect in that system?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I stated in evidence, in ideal circumstances, every death which does not have a doctor's medical certificate and an explanation, should be treated by the police as a suspicious death and investigated accordingly until such time as it is found to be otherwise. I'm not sure that that was entirely practical in these circumstances, but I do accept your suggestion that there were bodies buried in circumstances which I, as a police officer, would wish had not happened, because I think even bodies with some element of decomposition may yield information to investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, you said: "In ideal circumstances, every death which does not have a doctor's medical certificate ... should be treated as a suspicious death." I mean, you've seen the evidence. We're not talking about people being found dead in their beds without any sign of visible injury; we are talking about people on the ground with bullet-holes in their heads. Do you think it's a defect in the Croatian system at the time not to investigate deaths like that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And another -- at paragraph 3.62 of your report, you've concluded that: "... significant and serious crime there was. There were also significant detections, mostly of ethnic Croats and including soldiers and policemen as well as civilians." Now, just in terms of your -- the phrase "significant detections," you haven't conducted a comprehensive review of the evidence showing the actual commission of crime versus the investigation and punishment of crime that would allow you to make any reliable assessment as to the actual numbers of crimes committed in the area Sector South or the liberated area or the area of the indictment in this case, versus the number of cases that were dealt with appropriately by the authorities and detected, are you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the volume of material which I have seen is such, in terms of its magnitude, that I think it is difficult to make conclusions from it. And, of course, in terms of the more serious crimes, in some cases there is a dispute as to whether deaths were death through combat or deaths which arose after combat clearly had ceased in the area to which it refers. So, I think, in relation to these matters, there was difficulty with figures, which is why I have sought to assist the Chamber by judging that clearly there was a lot of crime going on, clearly there was a serious problem. There were different interpretations of how fires were caused; there were different interpretations of when and how people had died; but I don't think anyone is disputing that there was a lot wrong in what was happening here. And that, indeed, if we look at the activities of the courts, the prosecutors, the investigating judge, as well as the civilian police, we will see that action was taken in a number of these cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the document you cite in support of that conclusion is P600.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I'd like to look at that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this a document produced by Mr. Granic, the minister of foreign affairs, at a meeting on the 2nd of February, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 4 of that document in the English and the B/C/S. And it's at the bottom of both pages of this -- sorry, the bottom of the page in both the English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And is it states: "The accusations against the Croatian Army, to the effect that it has committed excessive human rights violations, are unfounded ... violations that occurred were not systematic, nor were such violations tolerated by government bodies. On the contrary, it must be point out that in" --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the pagination is out of order in this document, so we have to go to the following page in the English and the next page in the B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: "... in accordance with a highly developed awareness of the importance of the rule of law, criminal proceedings have been instituted against 80 members of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia ..." Now, do you have any idea whether instituting proceedings against 80 members of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia, in relation to crimes committed following the liberation of occupied territories up until January 1996, is either significant or insignificant, in terms of the overall number of violations of crime by HV members?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my judgement, which I suppose is subjective, it's significant. And I say that because not only does it involve 80 members of the Croatian armed forces, but investigations which would generate that sort of criminal justice activity will compass significantly more people. And if the argument is about well, Were the Croatian authorities taking this matter seriously or not? I suppose that must be -- ultimately that must be a judgement for this Chamber or even a political judgement. But what I can say from the perspective of a -- from a policing, civilian policing perspective, is that the sort of investigations which would lead to 80 members of the armed forces being tried will produce significant ripple effects, and that means that a lot of investigation must have taken place, a lot of people must have been looked at; and, therefore, in my view, the figure of 80 could be considered to be significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't say they've been tried. It says: "Criminal proceedings have been instituted against." And I'm wondering how you can conclude that that will produce significant ripple effects. What's the basis for that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you cannot -- if you're going to start criminal proceedings against 80 people, you have to ask a lot more than 80 people a lot of questions and conduct significant inquiries to generate the sort of evidence which you need to start proceedings against 80 people. There are only three people in the dock in this Chamber, but an awful lot of people have been impacted by the activities which led to the current proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: But you can't say whether these 80 people were just 80 HV members who were stopped at a check-point with looted goods and a criminal report was filed and possibly an indictment issued. I mean, you don't know the extent of --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... I -- no -- counsel, you're quite right. I don't know the individual circumstances of the cases of these 80 people. That's quite right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could look at the bottom of this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In the last paragraph it states: "With respect to the report by the secretary-general concerning the killings of civilians, the government of the Republic of Croatia should like to point out that, in most cases, these were casualties of military activities. This has been established by on-site inspection and the subsequent forensic investigation of corpses that were discovered." Now, this statement about on-site inspection and subsequent forensic investigation, that's not consistent with the evidence you've reviewed and the large volume of evidence received by this Trial Chamber that, in most cases, there were no such on-site investigations or forensic investigations. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would certainly agree that that paragraph, which you've just quoted, exaggerates the position, significantly, from the perspective of the government.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page of this document. If we could move down the page a little bit. That's great.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You can see the paragraph near the bottom of the page that states -- begins: "Regarding the murder of five civilians in the village of Grubor, the site of the crime was inspected by police on the same day on which it was reported by the UN Human Rights Action Team on 25 August 1995. However, the perpetrators have yet to be identified." Now, the evidence that you have reviewed indicated that the police did not inspect the crime scene at Grubori and the victims' bodies were sanitised and no investigation took place. Right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, I'm wondering, in light of the contradictions between what's stated in this document and the evidence you reviewed, why it is that you chose to rely on this document to support your conclusion about significant detections. What was the methodological basis for that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is significant material on the killings at Grubori. If I had decided to concentrate on that issue as a feature for my report, I feel it would have required significant detail. And it was my judgement, when I was compiling my report, that the Grubori incident did not impact sufficiently on the issues which I was addressing - namely, the connections between General Cermak and civilian policing - to warrant such an examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That wasn't exactly my question. And I will try to make it clearer. From what I have read to you - and it appears you agree with me - that there are indications in this document that it's not reliable, on certain issues, in contrast to other evidence that you have reviewed, and I'm wondering, in light of those indicia of unreliability, why you, nevertheless, chose to rely on this document in your report? It was more a methodological question.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I hoped that the answer was a methodological answer, but if not, then let me try to approach it from a different way. If the area that you're asking me about at this stage is contradictions between the pronouncements of the government of the Croatia on its performance in relation to the handling of crime matters and the evidence before the Chamber and the suggestion that there's a contradiction there and that the Grubori incident is related that, I agree with that. It wasn't something that I thought needed to feature in my report in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes. But you have relied on this document as support for conclusions about the performance of the government of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm wondering why you did that, in light of contradictions between what they say their performance was and what the other evidence indicates it actually was.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm sorry. I follow that now. Yes, I rely on this document as I rely on a number of other documents to make some general conclusions which are that there was a criminal justice system in operation and that some of the people that were caught up by that criminal justice system were, indeed, ethnic Croats and members of the HV. There are other documents, which I cite, to indicate that a criminal justice process involving the civilian police and the courts was taking place. I certainly don't want to suggest to this Chamber that I believe everything that the Croatian government would say, because they have political reasons and other agendas operating. I accept that entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, I'd just like to ask you a couple of questions about the civilian police manpower and resource issues which we touched on a few moments ago. And I'd like to go back to that. And that's at paragraph 3.104, and following, of your report. And it's my understand that you conclude that the shortage of manpower and other resources is a factor contributing to the level of crime and the lack of a response to reports of crime. And the example I pointed to earlier was at 3.115. Is that a fair understanding?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Any discussion of police manpower issues is fraught with difficulty, and police leaders will always want more resources than they have in order to deliver a better service than they're delivering, but I have attempted, in this report, to snap-shot some indications of what might be some of the problems facing police commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And faced with a manpower and resource issues, would you agree that, after Operation Storm, the police should have focused its resources, in a way, aimed at addressing the most serious and immediate problems of crime in the area?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And would you agree that, based on what you reviewed, the most serious and immediate problem of crime in the area after Operation Storm was looting, burning and killing?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So in -- going back to the practice we discussed of not investigating killing victims, would you agree that that is something that's inconsistent with what you think the focus of the police activity should have been?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it's -- it's a very disappointing outcome. But I think we have to understand that before you can start investigating crime scenes and carrying out -- not just on-site investigations but follow-up investigations to serious crime, you have to establish control over the territory in which you're operating. This is not a problem which is relevant for most civilian police forces, but for police forces operating either in areas of conflict or in areas which are immediately post-conflict. There are significant difficulties in establishing that sort of control. This is it why, in many areas, you have this difficulty over who has the primary responsibility for securing a safe and secure environment and maintaining civilian law and order. And in this particular area, the first necessity for the police is to establish an effective uniformed branch, civilian policing presence, so that roadblocks and the protection of individuals and buildings and people can be established so that roads can be secured with the assistance of the explosives ordnance people in the military to ensure that can you get from one place to another without driving over a mine. Then, you can seek to establish your control of crime scenes, your control of towns and villages in which you wish to conduct investigations and so on. I don't, for one moment, suggest that it would be wrong to criticise the performance of police either in individual cases or in some cases overall in terms of the successes that were achieved. What I say was there was a system which they were gradually establishing and putting in place, and that it's perhaps difficult, in the calm of the aftermath, to empathise with the actual practical difficulties which face people in trying to do this sort of thing. I have some experience of it myself, and whilst, as the Chamber heard earlier, I'm the first to criticise the absence of effective investigation of serious crime, I do have some sympathy with the difficulties which were facing the police at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Just to go back to the beginning of your answer which was related to control of the territory. If the MUP was able to send a civilian protection team to a site of a killing victim and collect that body and take it to a cemetery in Knin or Gracac and bury it, presumably, control of the territory wasn't an obstacle to actually investigating that crime or performing a forensic analysis of that body, was it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTOPHER ALBISTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, actually, I don't think that that is right. I don't think that does necessarily follow. There are documents which suggest that there was a concern amongst the civilian police, certainly, and maybe in other quarters, about the continuing existence of what are described variously as terrorists, Chetniks, and so on. Now, I don't attach too much weight to that, because I think that the Chamber may think there are reasons why those sorts of expressions are used and why such documents exist. Nevertheless, I don't think you can entirely dismiss the concerns which the civilian police may have felt about their own security in this region at this time. This was period of significant disorders, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Albiston, I get the impression that Ms. Gustafson is asking you about a specific example in which, due to the fact that MUP was, as she said, able to send a civilian protection team to a site of a killing victim and collect that body, that if you can do this, at that moment, at that place, you could send someone also to do a forensic investigation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, well, I'm sorry if my answer appears to be rather longer than it need be. But what I'm trying to explain to the Chamber, Mr. President, is that I don't know the example to which Ms. Gustafson is referring, but it is quite possible that you can get a team in, do a quick job, and get it out again without threat of violence to that teem. What I'm saying is that it would be wrong to extrapolate from a single instant, in which such an operation was carried out successfully, that, therefore, you could always do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that is not what Ms. Gustafson asked you. She didn't ask, If this happened, would that mean that you could go everywhere. She said, If you could go there to do this, couldn't you then have sent another person to investigate the crime. That was the question, at least if I understood you well, Ms. Gustafson. And you're making it -- in your answer you're making it far broader. That's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry. That does --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... it's definitely, it's the -- what struck me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see. Well, I -- certainly, in that case, I misunderstood the question. I would ask if the question could be put again so that I can deal with it directly in the way that Ms. Gustafson is seeking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I do so, I'm also looking at the clock. It's 16 minutes to 2.00. I would like to briefly discuss with the parties what time would still be needed, as matters stand now. I think we could do it in the presence of the witness, because then he knows already what his fate might be for the days to come. Ms. Gustafson, how much more time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: For my part, five to ten more minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five to ten more minutes. For re-examination, Ms. Higgins?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as it stands approximately 50 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm reading -- yes, it's 50. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I have a half an hour, maybe 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you would need that time to -- for matters that were raised in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And which you -- and which are not dealt with in examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There were touched upon in examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because we expect you to cross-examine the witness on matters that have been dealt with in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think that, in dealing with these issues, and I think great leave has been given, for instance, to the Prosecutor during their case, when issues have come up that are of some substance that need clarity, and I believe I will briefly deal with these issues that need some clarity, that we have been somewhat expansive on those rules Your Honour. So I'm not going to cover anything that hasn't been addressed to some degree, but on cross-examination, certain issues have been left out there that need some clarification for this witness's testimony to be complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you saying that if matters are left in cross-examination by the Prosecution, where you have had an opportunity to cross-examine the witness on whatever, you would like, then, to fill that, what you consider to be a gap, then that should be dealt with in cross then?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. If I can just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, what I'm say is, of course, the Chamber expects you to cross-examine the witness on any matter you consider of importance dealt with in examination-in-chief or to deal with any matter for which you think the witness could tell us about and which would support your case under Rule 90(H). Now, Ms. Gustafson has cross-examined the witness. And it's not entirely clear what matters you'd like that deal with in cross-examination. And my primary question was whether you would deal with any matter which was not addressed in examination-in-chief. And then you said something that matters that were not addressed in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No. I believe Mr. President, I may have misspoke. But there were issued that were raised in cross-examination that broadly may have been issued on direct but were specifically addressed by Ms. Gustafson. And my questions are related to those particular issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll see. If you would please keep in mind the concern I just expressed about what should and should not be covered in cross-examination and give that some consideration. Which means that, all together, that -- let me just ... One second, please. That would mean that we finish the re-examination by Ms. Higgins well within the first session tomorrow morning and that we would need another little bit of the next session, then, for you, Mr. Kehoe. Which also requires the next witness to be ready. He is on stand by, Mr. Kay. Then we will adjourn for the day. And we will resume tomorrow, Friday, the 6th of November, at 9.00, in Courtroom III. But not until I've instructed you, Mr. Albiston, that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, either already given or still to be given. The same instruction as I gave you before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 6th day of November, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 25
